stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother, who became concerned on her own after about three weeks of persistent cough and noticing he has fallen off his growth curve over the past two months; he was not identified through any screening program. No known TB contact in the household. No prior TB treatment, no known drug-resistant contact. Chest X-ray shows a hilar lymph node pattern suggestive of primary TB, without cavitation or miliary spread. Repeated attempts at gastric aspirate and induced sputum were both negative on molecular testing and smear. He has no HIV risk factors and no suspicion of drug-resistant TB. Exam: mild wasting, no respiratory distress, no lymphadenopathy outside the chest findings.

patient.social_history: Lives with mother; brought in on her own initiative, not through a screening program
patient.presenting_complaint: Persistent cough and growth faltering, noticed by his mother
patient.exam_findings: Mild wasting, no respiratory distress, hilar lymphadenopathy on imaging, no palpable lymphadenopathy
patient.prior_treatment: None for this episode; no prior TB treatment ever

distractors: His mother's own concern, without a specific triggering symptom she can pinpoint, treated as too vague to warrant urgent evaluation
The growth faltering attributed to normal variation in a preschool-age child rather than investigated as a possible sign of chronic illness
ntep_correct_actions: Recognize that even though this child was brought in by his mother's own initiative rather than through an active case-finding drive, NTEP's policy is to run active case-finding as standing, unconditional program activity across defined risk groups -- his case simply happened to be identified through passive presentation instead.
Start this child, who has non-severe disease without evidence of drug resistance, on the standard 6-month regimen (2HRZE/4HRE); no shorter regimen is offered regardless of severity.

Diagnose this child using clinical judgment: the highly suggestive imaging pattern (hilar lymphadenopathy) together with the negative bacteriological results and supportive clues is sufficient to diagnose clinically-diagnosed TB, without a defined, weighted scoring tool.
who_correct_actions: Recognize that this child's passive, mother-initiated presentation -- rather than identification through an active screening program -- is consistent with WHO's own conditional approach: general-population active case-finding is only recommended where local TB prevalence has been shown to meet a specific threshold (approximately 0.5% or higher), not as an unconditional activity.

Start this child on a 4-month regimen (2HRZ(E)/2HR) rather than the standard 6-month regimen, since he is between 3 months and 16 years of age with non-severe TB and no suspicion or evidence of MDR/RR-TB.

Consider using a structured integrated treatment-decision algorithm, which allocates evidence-based scores to microbiological, clinical, and radiological findings, as an option for diagnosing this child's presumptive pulmonary TB rather than relying solely on unstructured clinical judgment.
us_correct_actions: Attribute this child's case identification to his mother's own symptomatic concern, consistent with this framework's passive, contact-investigation-driven case-finding model rather than population-level active case-finding.
critical_error_conditions: Withholding any TB treatment from this child on the grounds that bacteriological confirmation was not obtained, despite highly suggestive imaging and an appropriate clinical diagnostic pathway
expected_divergence_points: Whether active case-finding is standing, unconditional national program policy or conditional on a demonstrated local prevalence threshold
Whether a 4-month or 6-month regimen is used for non-severe paediatric TB
Whether an unstructured clinical-judgment approach or a structured, scored treatment-decision algorithm is used to diagnose bacteriologically-unconfirmed paediatric TB
